children: 1224 ET - Bitcoin and gold are two sides of the same coin, according to Steve Neamtz of Yorkville America in a note. He says bitcoin as 'digital gold" simply doesn't have the benefit of time in the market to determine how it may behave in the course of financial stress, whereas gold has had thousands of years to "demonstrate its value as a reserve asset." But both will work for investors attempting to hedge against currency debasement. "None of this requires picking a side," he says. "Central banks are buying gold on infrastructure that already exists; institutions are buying bitcoin on infrastructure still being built--the same debasement logic, two different stages." Bitcoin falls 1.9%, while gold is off 1.6%. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

1100 ET - Dubai's residential property market faces pressure from an expected increase in housing supply over the next two years, S&P Global Ratings says. The emirate's housing stock could expand by around 20% through 2028, while Abu Dhabi could add approximately 13%, assuming construction projects proceed without delays, the ratings firm says, citing JLL estimates. The additional supply could constrain a recovery in property prices and rents. S&P also maintains negative rating outlooks on PNC Investments, associated with Sobha, and Omniyat Holding, citing their Dubai exposure and uncertainty surrounding the residential market. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

1044 ET - One of the only good features of the current run of elevated inflation is the cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security beneficiaries, Harris Financial Group's Jamie Cox says. The Social Security Administration just said benefits are set to rise by 3.6% in 2027, the biggest upward adjustment since 2023. Gasoline and energy prices are the proximate and temporary causes of the current run-up in inflation, so Social Security recipients could end up with a real, meaningful increase in benefits when the energy supply shock finally winds down, Cox says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1030 ET - Dubai's inflation rate is likely to rise again in October after easing to 5.0% in September from 5.5% in August, Emirates NBD Research says. The decline largely reflected a sharp fall in volatile recreation and culture prices rather than a broad easing in price pressures, economist Daniel Richards says. Recreation and culture prices fell 13.8% on month and 8.2% on year, while food, housing and transport costs remained elevated. Higher petrol prices are expected to push inflation up again, with Emirates NBD forecasting the annual rate at around 5.6% by the end of 2026. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

1019 ET - The median pay package among Canadian CEOs climbed 11.8% in 2025, the biggest annual increase three years, ISS-Corporate calculates. Compensation revealed during the 2026 proxy season showed the rise was driven largely by higher long-term incentive awards, which represented 60% of median total CEO pay, ISS-Corporate says. Base salary accounted for a small portion of total compensation, with the median CEO pay for 2025 about C$6 million. The data shows elevated compensation increases were met with investor approval, with shareholder approval reaching 96% in the latest proxy season. (robb.stewart@wsj.com)

1016 ET - There were an estimated 62.6% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in September, Redfin says. The margin is up sharply from 56.9% in August. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer's market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville and a handful of Texas areas. When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. High housing costs and widespread economic uncertainty have caused many would-be buyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance of buyers and sellers today. There were an estimated 928,892 homebuyers in the market nationwide in September. That's down 2.4% from a month earlier, the fifth straight monthly decline. On the flip side, there were an estimated 1.5M home sellers in the market. That's up 1.2% month over month. (chris.wack@wsj.com)

1002 ET - Inflation is still gas-powered right now, but the pressures are filtering into other categories, including apparel and autos, LPL Financial's Jeffrey Roach says in a note. Gas prices rose 9.1% in September, which accounted for more than half of the monthly increase in consumer prices, he says. But that category is highly volatile and can reverse quickly, the economist says. Core inflation meanwhile rose 0.3%, pushing the annual rate up to 2.6% from 2.4% the prior month. That core measure needs to consistently run in the 0.1% to 0.2% range before markets can conclude that inflation pressures are contained, Roach says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

0950 ET - Investors will be paying special attention to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's appearance at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting in Bangkok on Friday after the September CPI data revived the prospects of an October rate hike, BMO analysts say in a note. While forwarded guidance isn't guaranteed, Warsh has shown a willingness to provide implicit signals about the future path of policy rates in his recent public appearances, the analysts say. They think the odds of an October hike is now "near a toss-up." (dean.seal@wsj.com)

0936 ET - Bitcoin is now down 1.1% to $82,457, tumbling after being up around $84,000 earlier this morning. A hotter-than-expected September CPI pushed the probability of an October Fed hike to 50% based on the CME FedWatch tool. The CPI news is hitting cryptocurrencies and other assets considered riskier. "The pass-through of higher energy costs into other 'core' items may be occurring more rapidly than previously thought," says Stephen Coltman of 21shares in a note. Ethereum falls 1.9% to $2,463, XRP is down 1.2% to $1.35, and solana slides 2% to $104.92. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

0922 ET - The warmer-than-expected core inflation data bolsters the case for more rate increases, but likely wasn't hot enough to warrant an October hike, Franklin Templeton Institute's Jeff Schulze says in a note. The data comes after dovish comments from top Federal Reserve officials that suggest the bar is high for a hike at the upcoming FOMC meeting this month, the strategist says. Still, today's data should be a modest headwind to risk assets, Schulze says. Expectations for near-term rate hikes put pressure on the long end of the yield curve, strengthening the dollar while weighing on equity valuations, he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

0918 ET - Following a firmer consumer inflation report, economists and Federal Reserve officials will turn their attention to two other key economic releases this week: wholesale inflation and retail sales. Economists polled by WSJ expect September wholesale inflation to rise 5.5% from a year earlier, up from 5.4% in August. With both the CPI and PPI reports in hand, economists will calculate their forecasts for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. Bank of America expects September retail sales to come in slightly above consensus, reflecting resilient consumer spending. Some Fed officials have pointed to robust consumer spending as a sign of broader economic strength.(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

0911 ET - Expectations for higher interest rates rise sharply following the September CPI print. Markets are pricing in a 95.7% probability of at least one rate hike by the Fed's December meeting, according to CME FedWatch. For October, the probability of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike rises to 49.3%, from 22.1% Tuesday. Following Thursday's wholesale inflation report, economists will begin submitting their forecasts for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. (jessica.coacci@wsj.com)
